title: Hermanowski v. Acton Corp. — trial judgment and limited appellate remand
lead: An executive kept a five-year stock option alive despite attempted cancellation and exercised after the stock rose. Liability survived appeal, but the aggregate exercise price required a limited remand.

actors.name: Charles Hermanowski
actors.role: Former Acton chairman, president and chief executive

actors.name: Acton Corporation
actors.role: Company promising a resignation-related stock option

actors.name: Judge Glasser
actors.role: District judge conducting the diversity bench trial

actors.name: Second Circuit panel
actors.role: Judges Meskill, Pierce and Pratt, issuing a per curiam decision

proceedings: District court found an irrevocable option, breach in November 1979, and $415,030 damages plus interest; unsupported counterclaims were dismissed.
Second Circuit affirmed liability and valuation method but remanded solely for reconsideration of the exercise-price subtraction.
limits: The actual district award and limited remand differ from the assignment’s simplified prices and unqualified “affirmed” description.
The appellate court did not itself award a $21,000 increase.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Resignation is exchanged for cash and an option
paragraphs: Charles Hermanowski’s March 1973 employment agreement made him Acton Corporation’s chairman, president and chief executive at $65,000 annually through December 31, 1976. At an April 11, 1975 board meeting at his home, he said resignation would serve the company’s interests. The board accepted and resolved, in consideration of ending the employment agreement, to pay $25,000 and grant a five-year nonqualified option for 50,000 common shares at $2 each. Company counsel prepared a handwritten agreement signed that evening, referring to Acton’s 1972 nonqualified stock plan.

Acton had two plans. Its qualified plan automatically ended options on employment termination or death. The nonqualified plan allowed cancellation at employment’s end, within a year by notice, or thereafter on thirty days’ notice. After repeated requests, Hermanowski received option certificates in December 1975 bearing an April date and reciting cancellation rights. He signed subject to an express noncancelability proviso and returned a copy with a rejecting letter.

Acton first responded in June 1976, asserting cancellability and giving thirty days’ termination notice. Hermanowski objected in July and September, without response. On September 28, 1979, within five years, he sent a $10,000 bank check to exercise for 5,000 shares. Acton returned it with a November 9 letter stating that it found no exercisable option. He learned of that rejection November 12.

sections.title: The trial judge finds a genuine five-year promise
sections.cue: Resolve the plan-reference ambiguity through the negotiations.
paragraphs: After a diversity bench trial, Judge Glasser rejected Acton’s contention that the plan reference incorporated every cancellation provision. Hermanowski explained that the reference avoided the qualified plan’s automatic termination consequence, rather than allowing Acton to cancel the consideration for his resignation. The judge found it implausible that an experienced executive would surrender approximately $100,000 of remaining salary for $25,000 and an illusory option.

The reference was also ambiguous, permitting negotiation evidence. Directors Mamber and Koehl testified that the intended option was noncancelable for five years. Mamber described a cash-poor company settling cheaply while letting Hermanowski share in its future. Koehl had proposed the board resolution. Neither knew the plan provisions or gave the hastily included reference special significance. The judge found an irrevocable option for 50,000 unregistered common shares at $2.

sections.title: The option holder chooses when to treat refusal as breach
sections.cue: Explain why the earlier cancellation did not set damages.
paragraphs: Acton argued that breach occurred with the December 1975 certificate or, at latest, the June 1976 notice. The judge refused to let that unilateral action force an early valuation date. An option was an irrevocable offer: Acton had to perform upon election, while Hermanowski remained free to exercise or decline. Good-faith belief in a cancellation right did not excuse repudiation.

Hermanowski could treat repudiation as present breach, seek performance or retraction, or ignore it until choosing to exercise. His 1976 letters sought restoration or the employment balance and threatened suit, but he ultimately retained and later exercised the option. Acton’s refusal in November 1979 breached the obligation as to all available shares, not just the first 5,000. Further demands or tenders were futile. The liability finding implicitly included readiness, willingness and ability to perform. Acton could have retracted by delivering shares but insisted it owed none. Giving it the earlier date would remove the very opportunity to speculate that the option supplied.

sections.title: Ordinary contract valuation produces the trial award
sections.cue: Distinguish the actual calculation from conversion damages.
paragraphs: Hermanowski requested the highest intermediate market price within a reasonable period after breach. The judge distinguished conversion cases, which compensate owners deprived of stock or control and allow time to replace it. Acton had broken a delivery promise, not converted shares Hermanowski already owned. Contract damages therefore measured lost gain at the time and place of breach.

Two ten-percent stock dividends increased the option to 60,500 shares. On November 12, 1979, the high and low market prices were $12.125 and $11.50, averaging $11.8125. Both experts accepted a discount for restricted shares, proposing twenty-five and thirty percent. The judge selected twenty-five percent and fixed value at $8.86 a share, or $536,030. He then subtracted $121,000 as the option price and awarded $415,030 plus statutory interest from November 12. His August 10, 1983 judgment also dismissed Acton’s unsupported counterclaims.

sections.title: The appeal preserves liability but questions the subtraction
sections.cue: End with the limited unresolved calculation.
paragraphs: On March 7, 1984, Judges Meskill, Pierce and Pratt issued a per curiam Second Circuit decision affirming against Acton but granting a limited remand on Hermanowski’s cross-appeal. They adopted the liability reasoning and approved the November 12 breach date and market-value-minus-exercise-price measure.

The question was multiplying $2 by the dividend-adjusted 60,500 shares. Hermanowski maintained that the original aggregate exercise price stayed $100,000, which would increase damages by $21,000. The certificate authorized adjustment of both share numbers and prices for dividends. An apparently unanswered Rule 36 admission request, the district finding of proportionate adjustments, and Acton’s failure to dispute $100,000 in trial submissions supported reconsideration. Yet the panel could not exclude an evidentiary reason for $121,000. It allowed the district judge to use the existing record or additional evidence and enter an appropriate judgment, affirming everything else.

The classroom problem substitutes simpler prices: $3 at attempted cancellation, a later $5 peak, and $4 at exercise, without dividends or restrictions. Under the trial court’s breach-date approach, those hypothetical facts yield 50,000 times the $2 spread, or $100,000. That exercise is distinct from the actual $415,030 trial award and the appellate remand.
